rationale: A wins because it keeps three real stories separate: LCA data, coffee-chain default, and the ugly business tension. Its strongest line, "A 1,400-location chain makes Oatly the default non-dairy pour across the US Northeast," is a clean beat story with the right proof burden. B has sharp questions, but "Plant-based dairy's growth era is over — Oatly's quarter shows what the survival era looks like" is category punditry built on one company's update. That is how founders end up pitching a trend they cannot prove.
gaps_in_A: "Oatly wins its biggest pour-volume deal" invents a superlative and volume claim. The update says 1,400 locations and default non-dairy status, not biggest deal or actual pour volume.
"Facts it rests on: ... no price change at retail" is misplaced under the coffee-chain angle. Retail shelf price does not answer cafe surcharge or menu pricing.
It misses the sharper cost question: whether the 31% footprint reduction came from cheaper inputs tied to the same cost-cutting behind the plant closure.
"Decay: 24hr" on the LCA angle is a little too cramped. A real methodology or green-claims scrutiny piece can live longer than launch day if the report is available.
gaps_in_B: "Plant-based dairy's growth era is over" is an unsupported sector claim. The set admits it needs category data, which means it should not be a kept angle yet.

"Oatly is closing a plant and cutting its carbon footprint in the same quarter" blurs the fact. The update supports a lower per-liter footprint for one reformulated product, not a company-wide carbon-footprint cut.
"same quarter" and "Oatly's quarter" overstate timing. The update mentions last quarter's narrowing loss, but does not prove the rollout, closure, and loss all sit in the same quarter.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is premature. Its own question says "The 31% number is unpitchable without it," so fact-checking the LCA and chain confirmation comes first.
